title: How to identify and stay safe around harmful algal blooms in Pennsylvania waters
text:
How to identify and stay safe around harmful algal blooms in Pennsylvania waters
Green scum, streaks, or discolored water seen along Pennsylvania shorelines during the summer may indicate the presence of harmful algal blooms, according to information released on July 15. While not every patch of green is dangerous, some may be caused by cyanobacteria—also known as blue-green algae—which can pose health risks to people and animals.
Harmful algal blooms occur when cyanobacteria multiply rapidly due to a combination of excess nutrients, warm temperatures, sunlight, and calm water. These organisms are typically harmless at low levels but can become hazardous when they produce toxins that sicken humans, pets, or wildlife; create unpleasant tastes and odors in drinking water; discolor the water; or reduce oxygen levels leading to fish kills. "HABs can pose human and canine health risks through ingestion of contaminated water, inhalation of water droplets, or skin contact. Symptoms in humans may include skin irritation, respiratory discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Canine symptoms may include excessive salivation, fatigue, difficulty breathing, vomiting, diarrhea, and seizures. Death in canines is possible within hours to days after exposure," the article said.
To avoid exposure, residents are advised not to enter discolored waters or those with visible scums; follow posted advisories even if the water appears clear; keep pets and children away from suspected blooms; and rinse off with clean water after swimming. Checking current conditions using Pennsylvania's Harmful Algal Bloom Dashboard before visiting recreational waters is recommended.
The article provides guidance for distinguishing between harmless aquatic plants like duckweed—which has leaves and rootlets—and potential cyanobacterial blooms that appear as tiny particles forming surface scums or causing unusual discoloration such as bright green or milky hues. A simple float test using a clear container can help determine if buoyant material might be cyanobacteria but cannot confirm toxicity.
Reporting suspected harmful algal blooms should be done via the Pennsylvania Department of Health website. The article notes that nutrient pollution—mainly nitrogen and phosphorus from sources such as lawn fertilizer runoff or failing septic systems—is a primary cause behind bloom formation.
Residents are encouraged to help prevent HABs by following best practices for fertilizer application (the 4Rs: right source, rate, time and place), maintaining septic systems regularly, picking up pet waste promptly around homes and parks,
limiting livestock access to waterways,
and planting native vegetation along shorelines. Educational resources on this topic are available through Penn State Extension which delivers science-based education statewide through local offices,
digital tools,
and collaborations with government,
industry,
and nongovernment organizations, according to the official website.
